screens.title: Sampling-Based Motion Planning
screens.narratorSegment: In high-dimensional robot planning, explicitly building a full grid is often impossible. In this lesson we'll learn why sampling-based planners are the practical alternative, and we will compare the two primary families you will use: roadmap methods and tree-based planners. Sampling-based planners randomly sample configurations, keep only collision-free points, and connect them to form a roadmap or a tree. This approach does not enumerate every configuration; instead it builds a sparse representation that still captures connectivity. You will see how PRM precomputes a graph for many queries, why it requires a static environment, and how RRT grows a tree quickly when you only need a single path. We will also examine RRT* and how local rewiring improves path quality over time. By the end of the chapter you should know when to prefer A-star, PRM, RRT, or RRT*, how collision checking influences performance, and how iteration count affects path quality. Think about a six-joint robot arm: sampling avoids the explosion of nodes that a regular grid would create, and that is the practical reason sampling methods are essential. When might you accept a jagged path in exchange for faster planning?

screens.title: Why sampling is necessary
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by building a clear mental model of the core motivation: dimensionality. A configuration space for a robot maps every possible pose to a point; a six-joint arm gives a six-dimensional space, and a humanoid can reach dozens of dimensions. Grid-based search like A-star performs well in two or three dimensions because the number of nodes is manageable. But even with ten discrete steps per joint, a six-degree-of-freedom arm yields a million nodes, and a seven-degree system multiplies that further. Sampling-based planners avoid explicitly enumerating nodes by drawing random samples directly from the continuous C-space. They keep only valid, collision-free samples and connect them locally. The result is a sparse graph or tree that captures reachability without visiting every combination of joint values. A common misconception is that random sampling is arbitrary and unreliable; in fact, these methods are probabilistically complete. That means as you increase the number of samples, the probability of finding a path, if one exists, tends to one. A concrete example: a 6-DOF manipulator navigating around a table can be planned by sampling valid arm configurations near the obstacle boundaries; you will not attempt to grid the six-dimensional space. Key takeaway: sampling trades exhaustive enumeration for statistical coverage that scales to high dimensions. Reflect on a specific robot you know: how many degrees of freedom does it have, and why would a grid be infeasible?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Sampling replaces full discretization in high-dimensional configuration spaces, enabling tractable planning by probabilistic coverage instead of exact enumeration.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Why sampling is necessary
Definition
Curse of dimensionality
Grid-based search grows exponentially as degrees of freedom increase. Sampling avoids this by selecting representative configurations rather than enumerating every discrete cell.
Concrete example
Ten discretizations per joint: 6 joints → 10^6 nodes. Sampling focuses effort on reachable, collision-free regions instead.
Common misconception
Random sampling is not unreliable — probabilistic completeness means more samples increase the chance of success when a path exists.
Key takeaway
Sampling scales to high-dimensional C-spaces by trading completeness for probabilistic coverage and tractability.
Analogy
Exploring a city by walking samples
Rather than mapping every street block, you walk to representative points and check whether each is reachable from others. Over time these visits reveal the connected streets without mapping every corner.
Why it matters
  • Enables planning for manipulators and humanoids with many joints.
  • Reduces computation and memory compared to exponential grids.
  • Makes online planning possible in high-dimensional tasks.

screens.title: Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM)
screens.narratorSegment: PRM is a two-phase, multi-query planner. The construction phase is offline: sample N configurations from the C-space, keep the collision-free ones, and for each valid sample find its k nearest neighbors. For each neighbor, check whether the straight-line path between the two samples is collision-free; if it is, add an edge. This creates a roadmap graph that captures the free configuration connectivity. The query phase is online: given a start and a goal, find their nearest nodes in the roadmap and attempt to connect them if collision-free. Then search the roadmap using a graph search such as Dijkstra or A-star to find a shortest path along the roadmap. PRM performs well when the environment is static and many queries are required because the expensive collision checks are done upfront. A practical point is neighbor selection: using a k-nearest strategy balances local connectivity and cost. A common pitfall is attempting PRM in a changing environment without rebuilding the roadmap; edges can become invalid. Concrete example: build a roadmap for a manipulator in a factory aisle during setup, then reuse that roadmap for many pick tasks. Key takeaway: PRM shifts computation to an upfront phase to serve many fast queries later. Consider whether your environment is static enough to justify construction cost.

keyIdea.text: Construction: sample, validate, connect neighbors. Query: connect start/goal and run graph search over the roadmap.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM)
Construction phase
Sampling and connecting
  1. Sample N random configurations and keep only collision-free ones.
  2. For each valid sample find k nearest neighbors in C-space.
  3. Check straight-line connections for collisions; add edges when safe.
Concrete example
Precompute a roadmap for a pick-and-place area and reuse it for many grasp queries without rechecking the entire scene each time.
Query phase
Connect and search
Given start and goal, connect them to nearby roadmap nodes if collision-free, then run graph search to find a path across the roadmap.
MATLAB snippet
function roadmap = prm_construct(cspace, N, k)
    roadmap.nodes = [];
    roadmap.edges = {};

    % Sample N configurations
    for i = 1:N
        q = cspace.random_sample();
        if cspace.is_valid(q)
            roadmap.nodes = [roadmap.nodes; q];
        end
    end

    % Connect nearest neighbors
    for i = 1:size(roadmap.nodes, 1)
        neighbors = knn(roadmap.nodes, roadmap.nodes(i,:), k);
        for j = 1:length(neighbors)
            if cspace.is_collision_free(roadmap.nodes(i,:), roadmap.nodes(neighbors(j),:))
                roadmap.edges{i} = [roadmap.edges{i}, neighbors(j)];
            end
        end
    end
end
Common pitfall
Using PRM in a changing environment without rebuilding the roadmap leads to invalid edges and incorrect paths. Recompute or repair the roadmap when obstacles change.
Key Takeaway

PRM shifts expensive collision checking to an offline construction phase so many later queries become efficient.

screens.title: Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT)
screens.narratorSegment: RRT is a single-query planner tailored to quickly explore large continuous spaces. The core loop samples a random configuration, finds the nearest node in the existing tree, and 'steers' from that node toward the sample by a fixed step size. If the new motion segment is collision-free, the node is added and the tree grows. The algorithm continues for a fixed number of iterations or until a node reaches the goal region. A concrete example: in a 2D workspace with rectangular obstacles, RRT will rapidly create branches that extend into unexplored areas, often finding a feasible path quickly. Important parameters are the step size, which controls branch length and smoothness, and a maximum iteration count that bounds runtime. A common misconception is that RRT always finds short paths; in practice RRT tends to produce jagged, suboptimal routes and may require post-processing smoothing. Use RRT when you need a fast single path or when the environment can change frequently, because the tree is cheap to rebuild. Below is a canonical MATLAB-like code snippet that demonstrates the main loop. After you read it, try to identify where you would add a sampling bias toward the goal to speed convergence.

keyIdea.title: RRT essentials
keyIdea.text: RRT grows a tree by steering from the nearest node toward random samples; it's fast for single queries but typically returns suboptimal, jagged paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT)
Algorithm
Sampling, nearest, steer
  • Sample q_rand and find nearest q_near in the tree.
  • Compute q_new = steer(q_near, q_rand, step_size).
  • If path q_near→q_new is collision-free, add q_new with parent q_near.
  • Terminate if q_new reaches the goal region or iterations exhausted.
Practical tip
Goal biasing — occasionally choosing the goal as q_rand — increases the chance of reaching the goal quickly at little extra cost.
Canonical code
function tree = rrt(cspace, start, goal, max_iter, step_size)
    tree.nodes = start;
    tree.parent = 0;

    for i = 1:max_iter
        q_rand = cspace.random_sample();
        [q_near, idx_near] = nearest_neighbor(tree.nodes, q_rand);
        q_new = steer(q_near, q_rand, step_size);

        if cspace.is_collision_free(q_near, q_new)
            tree.nodes = [tree.nodes; q_new];
            tree.parent = [tree.parent; idx_near];

            if norm(q_new - goal) < step_size
                if cspace.is_collision_free(q_new, goal)
                    tree.nodes = [tree.nodes; goal];
                    tree.parent = [tree.parent; size(tree.nodes,1)-1];
                    return;
                end
            end
        end
    end
end
Misconception
RRT will not reliably find the shortest path; it finds a feasible path quickly but does not optimize path length without additional processing.
Key Takeaway

RRT gives a fast feasible solution for single-query planning but often requires smoothing or optimization for execution.

screens.title: RRT vs RRT*
screens.narratorSegment: RRT and RRT* share the same sampling and extension ideas, but differ in how they manage tree structure after inserting a node. RRT simply adds the new node with its nearest parent; this keeps iteration cost low and makes RRT very fast for single queries. RRT* adds two important steps: when inserting a node, it searches nearby nodes for the parent that minimizes cost from the start, and then it attempts to rewire neighbors to use the new node if it reduces their cost. This local optimization increases per-iteration computational cost, but as iterations grow the tree's paths improve and converge toward the optimal path — that is, RRT* is asymptotically optimal. A concrete scenario: plan a 2D point robot around several obstacles for a time-critical emergency maneuver; RRT gives a quick path that may be jagged, whereas RRT* yields better paths if you have time to run more iterations. A misconception is thinking that RRT* always produces better immediate results; early iterations of RRT* can still be inferior to RRT until sufficient rewiring occurs. Key takeaway: choose RRT for speed and RRT* when path quality matters and you can afford extra computation.

keyIdea.text: RRT prioritizes fast exploration; RRT* adds local optimizations that trade per-iteration time for convergence to optimal paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › RRT vs RRT*
RRT
Fast single-query exploration
Adds nodes quickly with minimal local computation. Good for dynamic scenes and when you need any feasible path fast.
RRT*
Local optimization and rewiring
Searches neighbors for optimal parent and rewires to reduce cost over time, so paths approach optimality as samples increase.
Trade-off table
Speed
RRT > RRT*: RRT has lower per-iteration cost.
Path quality
RRT* > RRT: RRT* improves cost with more iterations.
Use case
RRT for real-time needs; RRT* for offline planning when path cost matters.
Misconception
RRT* does not always beat RRT in early iterations; it needs many samples to converge.
Key Takeaway

Prefer RRT for speed and RRT* when you can afford more computation and desire improved path cost over time.

screens.title: Collision Checking and Validity Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Collision checking is the workhorse of sampling-based planners. Every sampled configuration must be validated, and every potential edge between samples requires a collision-free straight-line check. Because collision checks are performed often, they typically dominate computation time. Efficient collision testing strategies — such as bounding-volume hierarchies or lazy collision checking — are essential to practical performance. For example, PRM performs many collision checks during construction, while RRT performs fewer checks per iteration but may still sample many segments. A common optimization is lazy evaluation: add an edge to the structure without performing full collision checks, then verify edges only when they are part of a candidate path during query time. The trade-off is potential wasted edges that later fail; however, this can reduce upfront cost. A concrete scenario: building a PRM for a manipulator near many obstacles can trigger thousands of segment checks; using fast geometric tests early and deferring expensive, precise checks until needed improves throughput. Misconception: collision checking cannot be optimized — in reality, algorithmic techniques and spatial data structures drastically reduce cost. Key takeaway: analyze how many collision checks each planner will require and optimize or amortize them to meet real-time or offline constraints.

keyIdea.title: Collision cost
keyIdea.text: Collision checks are the dominant cost; practical planners use spatial data structures, lazy checks, and amortization strategies to reduce runtime.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Collision Checking and Validity
Why it matters
Collision tests dominate runtime
Every sample and every candidate edge requires a validity check. For manipulators this means checking many degrees-of-freedom across geometry, and naive checks become the bottleneck.
Optimization
Use bounding volumes, spatial hashing, and lazy collision checks to reduce expensive geometry tests.
Lazy checking
Defer detailed checks until a path candidate is found. This amortizes cost when many edges are never used.
Concrete scenario
A PRM for a manipulator near clutter requires thousands of segment checks. Pre-filtering with coarse collision geometry and then running precise checks only on promising edges speeds construction significantly.
Misconception
Believing collision checks cannot be optimized leads to slow planners. Proper spatial structures and lazy strategies are effective.
Key Takeaway

Count and reduce collision checks: choosing a planner means understanding its collision-check profile and optimizing accordingly.

screens.title: PRM construction details
screens.narratorSegment: Drilling into PRM construction reveals choices that affect coverage and connectivity. The simplest sampler draws uniform random configurations, but you can bias sampling toward narrow passages or obstacle boundaries to improve connectivity in critical areas. After sampling, keep only configurations that pass collision tests. Next is neighbor selection: a k-nearest strategy connects each node to its k closest samples using Euclidean distance in C-space. Choosing k too small risks disconnected components; choosing k too large increases construction time and collision checks. Another practical choice is using a radius-based neighborhood: connect nodes within a radius that scales with log of samples and workspace dimension. For each candidate neighbor, perform a straight-line collision test between the two configurations; many implementations discretize the segment into small steps for collision checking of articulated robots. A misconception is that more samples always solve connectivity—without good neighbor rules and targeted sampling, important narrow corridors can remain undiscovered. Concrete example: when building a roadmap for a manipulator in a shelf-filled environment bias sampling toward joint configurations that bring the end-effector near shelf openings. Key takeaway: sampler, neighbor rule, and collision test resolution together determine roadmap quality and cost. Consider how you'd set k and sampler bias for a narrow passage problem.

screens.title: MATLAB exercise: RRT and RRT* comparison
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity will solidify the differences between RRT and RRT*. Create a 2D workspace with 3 to 5 rectangular obstacles and define start at (1,1) and goal at (9,9). Implement RRT and RRT* with identical sampling and steering functions. Run each planner for 1000 iterations and plot the tree and final path. Then increase iterations to 5000 and repeat. You will observe that RRT typically finds a feasible path quickly but its path length does not systematically improve much with more iterations. RRT* rewires the tree locally and will show a clear reduction in path cost as iterations increase. Record path length as a function of iteration count for RRT* to visualize convergence. A common error is comparing runtimes without equalizing collision-check strategies; ensure both planners use the same collision resolution and sampling seeds where possible for fair comparison. Practical note: plotting intermediate trees helps to see rewiring in action for RRT*: edges are reconnected to shorter parents over time. After completing the plots, reflect: how many iterations are required before RRT* gives a meaningful improvement and is that acceptable for your application?

screens.title: Single-query vs Multi-query planners
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right planner comes down to the problem setup. If you face many queries in the same static environment — for example, a manipulator performing thousands of pick operations in a fixed bin — PRM excels because the expensive construction phase is amortized over many fast queries. If you need to plan a single path quickly or the environment changes often, RRT is a strong choice because it builds a tree on demand and requires less upfront work. If path quality matters and you can afford extra computation, RRT* is preferred: it improves path cost over many iterations via rewiring and optimal parent selection. Consider other practical constraints: collision-check cost, available C P U time, and whether you need deterministic optimality. A common misconception is believing multi-query planners are always better when you have many queries; if the environment shifts frequently or obstacles move, the roadmap validity degrades and rebuilding cost becomes a burden. Concrete example: in mobile robot navigation through a factory with frequent layout changes, an RRT-based online planner supports replanning, while a PRM would need rebuilding. Key takeaway: match the planner to query count, environment stability, and required path quality before implementing a solution.

fullNarratorScript:
In high-dimensional robot planning, explicitly building a full grid is often impossible. In this lesson we'll learn why sampling-based planners are the practical alternative, and we will compare the two primary families you will use: roadmap methods and tree-based planners. Sampling-based planners randomly sample configurations, keep only collision-free points, and connect them to form a roadmap or a tree. This approach does not enumerate every configuration; instead it builds a sparse representation that still captures connectivity. You will see how PRM precomputes a graph for many queries, why it requires a static environment, and how RRT grows a tree quickly when you only need a single path. We will also examine RRT* and how local rewiring improves path quality over time. By the end of the chapter you should know when to prefer A-star, PRM, RRT, or RRT*, how collision checking influences performance, and how iteration count affects path quality. Think about a six-joint robot arm: sampling avoids the explosion of nodes that a regular grid would create, and that is the practical reason sampling methods are essential. When might you accept a jagged path in exchange for faster planning?

In this set of objectives we will make explicit the skills and understanding you should gain. First, you will explain the Probabilistic Roadmap method, including its construction and query phases. That means you can describe how samples are chosen, how collision-free nodes are connected, and why a precomputed roadmap supports many queries. Second, you will implement the Rapidly-exploring Random Tree algorithm for single-query planning. This is a hands-on skill: you will write the sampling, nearest-neighbor lookup, steering by a fixed step, and collision checks. Third, you will understand RRT* and its asymptotic optimality: you should be able to describe rewiring and optimal parent selection, and why these additions let the tree approach the best possible path as iterations grow. Fourth, you will compare graph-based and sampling-based methods and choose the appropriate planner for a given problem, such as preferring A-star for low-dimensional grids and PRM or RRT for higher-dimensional spaces. Each objective ties to a practical task or explanation, so you can both reason about trade-offs and implement a working planner. By the end, you should justify a planner choice for a 7 degree-of-freedom arm and reason about iteration counts and collision-check cost.

Now let's expand each objective with what mastery looks like and why it matters. Explaining PRM means you can name the construction steps and explain why nearest-neighbor connections require collision checking; you also understand limitations such as the need for a static map. Implementing RRT means you can code sampling, a nearest-neighbor search, and the steer function with a fixed step size. You will also add collision checks and a termination condition. Understanding RRT* requires you to describe two algorithmic additions: selecting the best parent among nearby samples to minimize cost, and rewiring neighbors to use shorter paths when found. These local optimizations are what give RRT* its asymptotic optimality property. Finally, comparing methods requires you to reason about dimensionality, query counts, and environment dynamics: A-star is optimal in low-dimensional grids but impractical beyond a few degrees of freedom, PRM is efficient for many queries in a static map, and RRT/RRT* are better for single-query or changing scenes. For mastery produce a short MATLAB experiment showing path length decrease for RRT* with more iterations.

We begin by building a clear mental model of the core motivation: dimensionality. A configuration space for a robot maps every possible pose to a point; a six-joint arm gives a six-dimensional space, and a humanoid can reach dozens of dimensions. Grid-based search like A-star performs well in two or three dimensions because the number of nodes is manageable. But even with ten discrete steps per joint, a six-degree-of-freedom arm yields a million nodes, and a seven-degree system multiplies that further. Sampling-based planners avoid explicitly enumerating nodes by drawing random samples directly from the continuous C-space. They keep only valid, collision-free samples and connect them locally. The result is a sparse graph or tree that captures reachability without visiting every combination of joint values. A common misconception is that random sampling is arbitrary and unreliable; in fact, these methods are probabilistically complete. That means as you increase the number of samples, the probability of finding a path, if one exists, tends to one. A concrete example: a 6-DOF manipulator navigating around a table can be planned by sampling valid arm configurations near the obstacle boundaries; you will not attempt to grid the six-dimensional space. Key takeaway: sampling trades exhaustive enumeration for statistical coverage that scales to high dimensions. Reflect on a specific robot you know: how many degrees of freedom does it have, and why would a grid be infeasible?

PRM is a two-phase, multi-query planner. The construction phase is offline: sample N configurations from the C-space, keep the collision-free ones, and for each valid sample find its k nearest neighbors. For each neighbor, check whether the straight-line path between the two samples is collision-free; if it is, add an edge. This creates a roadmap graph that captures the free configuration connectivity. The query phase is online: given a start and a goal, find their nearest nodes in the roadmap and attempt to connect them if collision-free. Then search the roadmap using a graph search such as Dijkstra or A-star to find a shortest path along the roadmap. PRM performs well when the environment is static and many queries are required because the expensive collision checks are done upfront. A practical point is neighbor selection: using a k-nearest strategy balances local connectivity and cost. A common pitfall is attempting PRM in a changing environment without rebuilding the roadmap; edges can become invalid. Concrete example: build a roadmap for a manipulator in a factory aisle during setup, then reuse that roadmap for many pick tasks. Key takeaway: PRM shifts computation to an upfront phase to serve many fast queries later. Consider whether your environment is static enough to justify construction cost.

RRT is a single-query planner tailored to quickly explore large continuous spaces. The core loop samples a random configuration, finds the nearest node in the existing tree, and 'steers' from that node toward the sample by a fixed step size. If the new motion segment is collision-free, the node is added and the tree grows. The algorithm continues for a fixed number of iterations or until a node reaches the goal region. A concrete example: in a 2D workspace with rectangular obstacles, RRT will rapidly create branches that extend into unexplored areas, often finding a feasible path quickly. Important parameters are the step size, which controls branch length and smoothness, and a maximum iteration count that bounds runtime. A common misconception is that RRT always finds short paths; in practice RRT tends to produce jagged, suboptimal routes and may require post-processing smoothing. Use RRT when you need a fast single path or when the environment can change frequently, because the tree is cheap to rebuild. Below is a canonical MATLAB-like code snippet that demonstrates the main loop. After you read it, try to identify where you would add a sampling bias toward the goal to speed convergence.

RRT and RRT* share the same sampling and extension ideas, but differ in how they manage tree structure after inserting a node. RRT simply adds the new node with its nearest parent; this keeps iteration cost low and makes RRT very fast for single queries. RRT* adds two important steps: when inserting a node, it searches nearby nodes for the parent that minimizes cost from the start, and then it attempts to rewire neighbors to use the new node if it reduces their cost. This local optimization increases per-iteration computational cost, but as iterations grow the tree's paths improve and converge toward the optimal path — that is, RRT* is asymptotically optimal. A concrete scenario: plan a 2D point robot around several obstacles for a time-critical emergency maneuver; RRT gives a quick path that may be jagged, whereas RRT* yields better paths if you have time to run more iterations. A misconception is thinking that RRT* always produces better immediate results; early iterations of RRT* can still be inferior to RRT until sufficient rewiring occurs. Key takeaway: choose RRT for speed and RRT* when path quality matters and you can afford extra computation.

Collision checking is the workhorse of sampling-based planners. Every sampled configuration must be validated, and every potential edge between samples requires a collision-free straight-line check. Because collision checks are performed often, they typically dominate computation time. Efficient collision testing strategies — such as bounding-volume hierarchies or lazy collision checking — are essential to practical performance. For example, PRM performs many collision checks during construction, while RRT performs fewer checks per iteration but may still sample many segments. A common optimization is lazy evaluation: add an edge to the structure without performing full collision checks, then verify edges only when they are part of a candidate path during query time. The trade-off is potential wasted edges that later fail; however, this can reduce upfront cost. A concrete scenario: building a PRM for a manipulator near many obstacles can trigger thousands of segment checks; using fast geometric tests early and deferring expensive, precise checks until needed improves throughput. Misconception: collision checking cannot be optimized — in reality, algorithmic techniques and spatial data structures drastically reduce cost. Key takeaway: analyze how many collision checks each planner will require and optimize or amortize them to meet real-time or offline constraints.
